lines.text: Why this matters
A lakehouse lesson is useful only if you can explain the problem it is trying to solve. A data lake gives
inexpensive, flexible file storage, but files alone do not automatically provide table-level transactions,
dependable updates, or a trustworthy current snapshot. A warehouse gives strong table semantics
and SQL-oriented management, but traditionally asks you to load data into a managed analytical
system. A lakehouse combines lake-style object/file storage with a table format and transaction layer
so engineering teams can keep open data files while gaining reliable table behavior. The point is not
that one architecture wins every workload. The point is to choose the guarantees you need and know
which layer supplies them.
Picture it in your head
Picture three rooms. The first is a large storeroom where boxes can be placed cheaply: that is the
lake. The second is a carefully managed shop floor with labelled shelves, transactions, and controlled
access: that is the warehouse. The lakehouse keeps the large storeroom but adds a reliable inventory
ledger and table rules so readers can ask, 'What is the committed table right now?' without scanning
whatever files happen to exist. Delta Lake is one implementation of that table layer on top of lake
storage.
New words before we use them

rows: Object/file storage used for raw and processed data; flexibility is high, table guarantees depend on added systems.
Managed analytical database/platform with table semantics, SQL, governance and optimized serving.
Architecture that brings table/transaction capabilities to lake storage.
Metadata + rules that define which data files belong to a table snapshot and how changes are committed.
Atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability - properties used to reason about reliable transactions.

OPEN SOURCE - CLICK HERE
https://docs.delta.io/
Optional visual - no verified bounded range: Databricks - How Delta Lake Supercharges Data Lakes
Conceptual transaction-log/lakehouse walkthrough; version-specific commands may be old
OPEN SOURCE - CLICK HERE
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u1VfOiHVeMI
Follow with me once
Take the same business problem - daily order files plus late corrections - and design it three ways. In
a plain file lake, write down how a reader decides which files are current after a correction. In a
warehouse, write down where the corrected row is stored and what transaction semantics the
database supplies. In a lakehouse, keep the files in lake storage but let the table log decide the
committed snapshot. Do not use product names first; name the guarantee first.
# Reasoning exercise - no Delta runtime needed
for design in ['lake', 'warehouse', 'lakehouse']:
print(design, '-> storage / table-state contract / correction rule')
What you should see
You should be able to produce a three-column design note that separates storage from table
semantics. The lake column should not falsely promise updates or transactions just because the files
are Parquet. The warehouse column should acknowledge managed table behavior. The lakehouse
column should identify a table layer that tracks committed versions over lake files.
Why it worked
Example: orders arrive as Parquet each hour. At 14:00 an upstream correction changes order O17. If
consumers scan every file in a folder, they may see both old and corrected rows unless another
convention tells them which one wins. A Delta table records a new committed version whose
snapshot includes the files/actions representing the correction. Readers query the table snapshot, not
an accidental folder listing.
Break it / common failure
A common beginner failure is to call any collection of Parquet files a lakehouse. Parquet is a columnar
file format; it does not by itself provide a transaction log or table history. Another failure is saying a
lakehouse 'replaces warehouses.' Real architectures may use both, and the deciding factors include
workload, governance, latency, team skills, interoperability and cost.
Reason through a realistic incident
A reporting team says yesterday's revenue changed even though no report code changed. Storage
contains the original order files plus a late correction file. Ask: what is the table contract? Can you
identify one committed snapshot? Is duplicate/correction precedence encoded in a log/table
operation, or is every reader inventing its own rule? The incident is not solved by buying faster
storage; it is solved by clarifying state and commit semantics.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
Separate three questions in architecture reviews: where bytes live, how a table snapshot is defined,
and which compute engine reads/writes it. Lakehouse thinking becomes clearer when those layers
are not collapsed into one vendor name. In this module, Spark is the compute engine, Parquet
remains the underlying data-file format, and Delta adds table metadata/transaction semantics. That
layered mental model will make later Iceberg/Hudi comparisons easier without needing to learn them
now.
Now you do a changed version alone
Choose a fictitious logistics company receiving shipment events, corrections and daily aggregates.
Write one paragraph for lake, warehouse and lakehouse designs. For each, state where bytes live,
who decides the current truth, how a correction is applied, and what a reader must trust.
Fresh changed retry
Now change the scenario: the company has immutable compliance archives that are never updated.
Explain why a simple lake zone may be completely appropriate for that zone even if the curated
serving layer uses Delta tables.
Validation and recovery ladder
State the table grain and stable business key before changing data.
Record before/after row count, distinct key count and at least one business total or invariant.
Inspect table history/version evidence; do not infer committed state from physical file presence.
When a source batch can contain multiple rows per target key, make precedence deterministic or
stop on ambiguity.
Repair one cause at a time and rerun a changed case; never hide an unexplained mismatch with
overwrite or dropDuplicates.
Keep protected reviews closed until your genuine attempt and evidence are saved.
Ready-made revision
Lake, warehouse and lakehouse are architecture choices, not maturity ranks. A lakehouse keeps lake
storage but adds table-level metadata and transaction behavior. Always name the required
guarantee - current snapshot, update/delete, history, concurrency, schema control - before naming
the technology.
Evidence / mastery
Save the three-design comparison, the changed compliance scenario, and a 60-90 second
explain-back: 'Parquet files are not automatically a transactional table.' Mastery means you can state
which layer supplies each guarantee without marketing language.
Why this matters
M11 taught you file formats and M12 taught you distributed processing. Now the key transition is to
stop treating a directory as if it were a database table. A directory can contain valid Parquet files and
still have no atomic definition of 'the table at version 7.' Concurrent writers can leave multiple
candidate file sets, retries can duplicate output, and readers can observe a mix of old and new files if
the application has no commit protocol. Delta's table log turns file actions into a versioned snapshot
contract.
Picture it in your head
Imagine a restaurant kitchen receiving paper tickets. The food containers are data files. If tickets are
scattered on the floor, you can see containers but you do not know which orders were cancelled,
replaced or committed. The transaction log is the ordered ticket book. The current table is
reconstructed from committed add/remove actions, not from guessing based on filenames or
modification times.
New words before we use them

rows: The set of table metadata and data files that represent one committed version.
An atomic recorded table change that creates a new version if it succeeds.
Conceptual log actions that add a data file to or remove it from the current snapshot.
Directory containing Delta transaction-log information for a table.
Metadata indicating a file has been logically removed from the current table but may still exist physically until retention cleanup.

OPEN SOURCE - CLICK HERE

Follow with me once
Use `practice/delta/01_files_vs_tables.py` on the learner PC. The script writes the same tiny dataset
once as Parquet and once as Delta. Inspect the directory names. Do not edit `_delta_log`. Then
append one row to the Delta table and inspect history. Your goal is not to memorize filenames; it is to
connect a logical table version to recorded commit metadata.
parquet_path = BASE / 'parquet_orders'
delta_path = BASE / 'delta_orders'
df.write.mode('overwrite').parquet(str(parquet_path))
df.write.format('delta').mode('overwrite').save(str(delta_path))
print(list(delta_path.iterdir()))  # includes _delta_log
What you should see
The Parquet directory should contain data files and Spark metadata such as success markers
depending on the writer. The Delta directory should contain Parquet data files plus `_delta_log`. After
the append, the Delta table should have another history version. Reading the table through
`format('delta')` should return the committed logical rows rather than forcing your script to decide
which physical files are active.
Why it worked
Suppose version 0 adds files A and B. A correction creates version 1 that adds file C and logically
removes A. The current snapshot is B + C, even if A still exists on disk for time-travel/retention
reasons. A naive recursive Parquet reader might read A + B + C and produce wrong results. A Delta
reader consults the table log and uses the active snapshot.
Break it / common failure
Do not delete files manually because they 'look old.' Physical presence is not the same as logical
membership. Do not use filesystem modified time as a business version. Do not write unrelated files
inside a table directory and assume Delta will protect them from every maintenance operation.
Table-managed directories need a clear ownership boundary.
Reason through a realistic incident
A junior engineer compares storage size with current table size and says Delta duplicated data.
History shows an overwrite and the old files still exist. Diagnose correctly: logical removal can
precede physical cleanup so time travel and concurrent readers remain safe. Confirm current row/key
totals through the Delta snapshot before discussing retention or VACUUM.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
The important abstraction is not 'Delta has JSON files.' It is that readers and writers agree on a
protocol for constructing snapshots and committing changes. Checkpoints can compact log state for
efficient reconstruction; the details evolve across versions, but the contract remains: table state
comes from committed metadata, not folder intuition. This is why table formats matter for
interoperability - independent engines can implement the protocol rather than reverse-engineer one
application's filenames.
Now you do a changed version alone
Draw versions 0, 1 and 2 for a table using fictional files A-D. For each version, list add/remove actions
and calculate the active file set. Then explain why a raw folder scan at version 2 could be wrong if
removed files remain physically present.
Fresh changed retry
Change version 2 so a failed job produced an unreferenced Parquet file E without a successful
commit. Explain why 'file exists' is not enough to make E part of the table and why manual cleanup
must still respect retention/ownership rules.
Validation and recovery ladder
State the table grain and stable business key before changing data.
Record before/after row count, distinct key count and at least one business total or invariant.
Inspect table history/version evidence; do not infer committed state from physical file presence.
When a source batch can contain multiple rows per target key, make precedence deterministic or
stop on ambiguity.
Repair one cause at a time and rerun a changed case; never hide an unexplained mismatch with
overwrite or dropDuplicates.
Keep protected reviews closed until your genuine attempt and evidence are saved.
Ready-made revision
A file is a storage object; a table is a logical contract. Delta's transaction log records committed
actions and lets readers construct a snapshot. Current table membership is not determined by 'every
Parquet file in the directory.'
Evidence / mastery
Save the directory inspection, `DESCRIBE HISTORY`/history output, active-file paper exercise and
changed retry. If Delta did not run on your PC, mark runtime PENDING and use the supplied simulator
only as reasoning evidence.
Why this matters
ACID becomes useful when you connect each letter to a failure you have already seen. Atomicity
means a multi-file table change is committed as one logical operation or not exposed as a partial
table version. Consistency means declared table invariants are preserved across committed states.
Isolation means concurrent readers/writers reason about stable snapshots and conflicts rather than
half-written folder contents. Durability means a successful commit remains part of the table history
under the storage system's durability guarantees. Delta implements these ideas through an ordered
transaction log and versioned snapshots.
Picture it in your head
Think of a bank ledger. A transfer touches multiple balances, but customers should never observe a
state where money left account A and has not yet arrived in B. Delta's exact mechanics differ from a
bank database, but the mental picture is the same: the commit boundary defines what other readers
can consider real. Each successful table commit advances the version.
New words before we use them

rows: Expose all parts of a committed table change together, not a partial result.
Committed states respect table/protocol constraints and application invariants.
Concurrent operations see/produce controlled snapshots; conflicts are detected according to the protocol.
Once committed, state survives normal process failure subject to underlying storage durability.
Monotonically advancing committed table state used for history and time travel.
Writers proceed using a snapshot and validate conflicts when attempting to commit, rather than locking the whole table for the entire job.

Follow with me once
Run `02_transaction_log_versions.py`. It creates a small Delta table, performs an append and a
targeted update, then prints history. Before running, predict how many committed versions you
expect. After running, record operation names and verify the latest row/key totals. Do not infer
version numbers from how many Parquet files were written - one table commit may add/remove
several files.
delta = DeltaTable.forPath(spark, str(TABLE))
for row in delta.history().select('version','timestamp','operation').collect():
print(row)
What you should see
You should see sequential history versions for the completed operations. The latest snapshot should
reflect the updated business row exactly once. The number of physical files may differ from the
number of table versions, because versions represent commits, not files.
Why it worked
Suppose two writers both read version 5. Writer A updates partition/date X and commits version 6.
Writer B then tries to commit based on its earlier snapshot. Whether B can safely commit depends on
the actions/conflicts involved; the system must not silently combine incompatible changes into an
unexplained partial state. Your debugging evidence is table history and conflict/error information, not
'both jobs finished their Python loops.'
Break it / common failure
Do not claim ACID means no job can fail. Jobs fail; ACID helps define what becomes committed and
visible. Do not claim isolation means every writer is globally serialized from start to finish. Delta uses
optimistic concurrency patterns. Do not equate schema enforcement with every business-quality rule
- a string can be valid by schema and still contain an invalid customer code.
Reason through a realistic incident
A pipeline wrote several Parquet files and then crashed before its intended final state. A raw file
consumer sees some new files and some old ones. A Delta consumer still reads the latest committed
snapshot. Investigate whether a commit was recorded, what version became current, and whether
the crashed job should retry idempotently. The right question is not 'did some files get created?' but
'what table version committed?'
Deepen the engineering reasoning
Table history is operational evidence. It can answer which operation created a state, when, and often
metrics such as rows/files affected. That does not replace application-level audit columns or source
reconciliation, but it gives you a reliable table-state timeline. In production incident response,
combine three layers: source evidence, pipeline run evidence and table commit/history evidence. A
clean Delta history cannot prove the source delivered the right business data.
Now you do a changed version alone
Write a failure matrix for four cases: crash before commit, successful append, conflicting concurrent
update, and successful overwrite. For each, state what a reader should consider current and which
evidence you would inspect first.
Fresh changed retry
Change the scenario so two jobs touch disjoint date partitions. Explain why 'concurrent' does not
automatically mean 'conflict,' but why you should still rely on actual commit behavior and not
hard-code assumptions about every operation.
Validation and recovery ladder
State the table grain and stable business key before changing data.
Record before/after row count, distinct key count and at least one business total or invariant.
Inspect table history/version evidence; do not infer committed state from physical file presence.
When a source batch can contain multiple rows per target key, make precedence deterministic or
stop on ambiguity.
Repair one cause at a time and rerun a changed case; never hide an unexplained mismatch with
overwrite or dropDuplicates.
Keep protected reviews closed until your genuine attempt and evidence are saved.
Ready-made revision
Delta versions represent committed table states. ACID is about transaction visibility and correctness,
not immunity from failure. Debug from source -> job -> commit/history -> reconciled business
output.
Evidence / mastery
Save the version prediction, actual history, row/key totals, failure matrix and changed retry. Be able
to explain why file count and version count are different concepts.
Why this matters
A table format earns its place when common data-engineering changes can be expressed as table
operations instead of bespoke file-rewrite conventions. Delta supports creation, append/overwrite,
reads and DML-style update/delete operations. These operations are powerful because they create
new committed snapshots while retaining old files as needed for history/retention. Your responsibility
is to use precise predicates, reconcile the result, and understand that logical deletion is not
immediate secure erasure of every historical byte.
Picture it in your head
Think of editing a version-controlled spreadsheet where each accepted edit creates a new revision.
UPDATE changes matching records in the new revision. DELETE removes matching records from the
new logical view. The old revision may remain retrievable until retention cleanup. You should picture
a new table snapshot, not an in-place mutation of one Parquet row inside a file.
New words before we use them

rows: Data manipulation operations such as insert/update/delete/merge.
Boolean condition selecting rows to change.
Row is removed from current table state; historical files may still exist until cleanup.
Columnar files containing changed rows may be rewritten because Parquet files are immutable objects.
History fields that can help validate how many rows/files an operation affected.

https://docs.delta.io/delta-update/
Official: Delta Quick Start
Create/read/write/update patterns
OPEN SOURCE - CLICK HERE
https://docs.delta.io/quick-start/
Follow with me once
Run `03_crud.py`. It creates four orders, updates one status with a precise order_id predicate, deletes
one cancelled training row, then prints sorted output and history. Before each DML action, calculate
the expected row count, key set and amount sum. After each action, reconcile all three. A successful
API call is not your validation.
delta.update(condition="order_id = 'O2'", set={'status': "'closed'"})
delta.delete(condition="order_id = 'O4' AND status = 'cancelled'")
What you should see
The update should change only the intended order's status without changing row count or key set.
The delete should reduce row count by exactly one and remove exactly the expected key. History
should show the table operations. Your saved controls should make an accidental broad predicate
obvious.
Why it worked
If `UPDATE orders SET status='closed' WHERE order_id='O2'` targets one known key, you can prove
scope before and after. If instead a developer writes `WHERE status IS NOT NULL`, the command may
be syntactically valid and catastrophically broad. Engineering safety comes from previewing the
predicate population and storing reconciliation controls, not from trusting the operation name.
Break it / common failure
Never demonstrate UPDATE/DELETE on valuable data without a safe sandbox, predicate preview and
recovery plan. Do not tell a privacy stakeholder that DELETE immediately erases historical storage;
VACUUM/retention and governance policies matter. Avoid using overwrite as a casual substitute for a
targeted correction when it increases blast radius.
Reason through a realistic incident
A delete job intended to remove 120 test records reports 1.8 million rows affected. Stop before
maintenance cleanup. Preserve history, inspect the predicate and current/previous versions, and
determine whether a restore or corrected write is appropriate. Do not run VACUUM during
investigation because you may destroy the historical files needed for recovery.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
DML correctness has two dimensions: selection correctness and resulting-state correctness. Selection
correctness asks whether the predicate matched the intended population. Resulting-state correctness
asks whether keys, grain, totals and downstream constraints remain valid after the new commit.
Production runbooks should capture both, plus a rollback/restore decision path. Delta gives you table
mechanics; it does not know your business invariant unless you encode/check it.
Now you do a changed version alone
Extend the fixture with five shipments. Write one safe update and one safe delete. Before executing,
print the candidate rows. After executing, reconcile count, key set and a numeric total. Save evidence
showing the predicate could not affect unrelated rows.
Fresh changed retry
Change the delete requirement from a specific key to 'all records older than a cutoff except legally
retained customers.' Design the predicate preview and validation checks you would require before
allowing execution.
Validation and recovery ladder
State the table grain and stable business key before changing data.
Record before/after row count, distinct key count and at least one business total or invariant.
Inspect table history/version evidence; do not infer committed state from physical file presence.
When a source batch can contain multiple rows per target key, make precedence deterministic or
stop on ambiguity.
Repair one cause at a time and rerun a changed case; never hide an unexplained mismatch with
overwrite or dropDuplicates.
Keep protected reviews closed until your genuine attempt and evidence are saved.
Ready-made revision
Create/read/update/delete are table operations that produce committed snapshots. Precision comes
from predicate preview, row/key/amount reconciliation and history evidence. Logical deletion and
physical retention are different concerns.
Evidence / mastery
Save candidate-population previews, before/after controls, history rows and the changed
legal-retention design. Explain how you would recover from an overly broad DML operation before
retention cleanup.
Why this matters
Pipelines break when a producer changes structure without a contract. Delta schema enforcement
prevents many incompatible writes from silently changing a table. Schema evolution gives you
controlled ways to accept intentional structural change. The engineering skill is not 'turn
mergeSchema on.' It is deciding whether a change is compatible with the table's meaning, validating
downstream consumers, and recording the decision. Automatic evolution is a tool, not permission for
producers to mutate contracts freely.
Picture it in your head
Imagine a customs form with required fields. Enforcement is the officer rejecting a shipment whose
paperwork does not match the declared form. Evolution is formally updating the form when the
business adds a legitimate field. Leaving the gate permanently open because 'new columns might
appear' is not governance.
New words before we use them

rows: Reject/guard writes that do not match the target table structure according to Delta/Spark rules.
Intentional change to the target schema, such as adding columns through supported mechanisms.
Write option that can merge compatible incoming schema changes.
Option used in overwrite scenarios when replacing a schema intentionally; high blast radius.
Agreed structure and semantics between producers and consumers; broader than data types alone.

Optional video
Official: Delta batch reads and writes
Schema validation and schema update/evolution behavior
OPEN SOURCE - CLICK HERE
https://docs.delta.io/delta-batch/
Official: Delta Lake documentation
Schema enforcement as a core Delta capability
OPEN SOURCE - CLICK HERE
https://docs.delta.io/
Follow with me once
Run `04_schema_evolution.py`. First write a baseline customer table. Next attempt to append a
DataFrame containing a genuinely new column without enabling schema evolution and save the
expected failure. Then repeat using an explicit evolution option and inspect the resulting schema.
Finally reconcile old rows: the new column may be null for historical records unless you backfill it.
# First attempt should fail for an unexpected new column.
incoming.write.format('delta').mode('append').save(str(TABLE))
# After explicit approval:
incoming.write.format('delta').option('mergeSchema','true').mode('append').save(str(TABLE))
What you should see
The uncontrolled append should fail rather than silently changing the target. The controlled evolution
should add the new column. Historical rows should remain present and keys unchanged; the new field
should have a predictable value/null pattern. Record the exact schema before and after.
Why it worked
Adding nullable `loyalty_tier` can be a compatible business change if downstream consumers tolerate
it. Changing `customer_id` from a stable string identifier to an integer code is not 'just schema
evolution'; it may change key semantics. A type-compatible technical write can still violate the
business contract, so schema review must include meaning and downstream dependencies.
Break it / common failure
Do not globally enable auto-merge merely to eliminate schema errors. That can turn a useful failure
signal into silent drift. Do not use overwriteSchema as a first response to one bad batch. Do not treat
column presence as proof of valid data: a newly added field may be 100% null or populated with
malformed values.
Reason through a realistic incident
A producer deploys a new `discount_code` field Friday evening. The Silver table starts failing. Your
options include reject/quarantine until the contract is approved, evolve the schema with explicit
consumer checks, or route the field only in Bronze while curated layers remain stable. The wrong
response is to bypass enforcement without understanding which downstream jobs select `*`, serialize
fixed schemas or calculate hashes from all columns.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
Schema governance should distinguish additive, breaking and semantic changes. Additive does not
automatically mean harmless: column order assumptions, CSV exports, downstream strict schemas
and wildcard selects can still break. For important tables, store schema-change evidence alongside
deployment/runbook notes. Delta records table metadata changes, but team process decides
whether the change was authorized.
Now you do a changed version alone
Design an evolution request for an orders table adding `source_channel`. Specify owner,
nullable/default behavior, Bronze/Silver/Gold impact, backfill decision, validation query and rollback
plan. Then implement the change in the local training table.
Fresh changed retry
Change the request to rename a business-critical column used by dashboards. Explain why this is a
different risk class from adding a nullable field and how you would stage compatibility rather than
flipping it instantly.
Validation and recovery ladder
State the table grain and stable business key before changing data.
Record before/after row count, distinct key count and at least one business total or invariant.
Inspect table history/version evidence; do not infer committed state from physical file presence.
When a source batch can contain multiple rows per target key, make precedence deterministic or
stop on ambiguity.
Repair one cause at a time and rerun a changed case; never hide an unexplained mismatch with
overwrite or dropDuplicates.
Keep protected reviews closed until your genuine attempt and evidence are saved.
Ready-made revision
Enforcement makes drift visible; evolution makes approved change possible. Never confuse
'supported by the engine' with 'safe for the business contract.' Validate schema, keys, null behavior
and consumers.
Evidence / mastery
Save the intentional failed write, before/after schemas, key reconciliation, evolution request and
changed rename plan. Mastery means you can defend when to reject, evolve or quarantine.
Why this matters
When a result changes, engineers need to reproduce what a table looked like at a known point. Delta
time travel lets you read previous snapshots by version or timestamp while retained data/log history
remains available. This supports debugging, audit investigation and reproducible backfills. It is not an
infinite backup system: retention and VACUUM can remove files needed for older versions. Version
history is evidence with a lifetime.
Picture it in your head
Picture a stack of transparent maps. Version 0 shows the first road network. Version 1 adds a bridge.
Version 2 closes a road. Time travel chooses one map layer without pretending the newer layers
never happened. VACUUM can eventually discard old physical pieces, so an old map may no longer
be reconstructable forever.
New words before we use them

rows: Read a previous table snapshot by version or timestamp.
Policy controlling how long historical log/data files remain available for reconstruction.
Maintenance operation that removes unreferenced data files older than a retention threshold.
Create a new commit that makes an earlier table state current again; different from simply reading an old version.

Official: Delta Quick Start - time travel
Reading earlier versions
OPEN SOURCE - CLICK HERE
https://docs.delta.io/quick-start/
Official: Delta batch reads/writes - retention and time travel
Retention boundaries for historical access
OPEN SOURCE - CLICK HERE
https://docs.delta.io/delta-batch/
Official: Delta utility commands
History and restore operations
OPEN SOURCE - CLICK HERE
https://docs.delta.io/delta-utility/
Follow with me once
Run `05_time_travel.py`. It creates version 0, appends a change to make version 1, then reads both
snapshots and prints history. Write down a control for each version before looking at output. Do not
run VACUUM as part of this lesson. The objective is to prove reproducibility, not storage cleanup.
v0 = spark.read.format('delta').option('versionAsOf', 0).load(str(TABLE))
latest = spark.read.format('delta').load(str(TABLE))
DeltaTable.forPath(spark, str(TABLE)).history().show(truncate=False)
What you should see
Version 0 should return the original key set and totals; the latest version should include the appended
change. History should show both commits. Your evidence should clearly label which query used an
explicit historical version and which used current state.
Why it worked
A finance report generated from table version 42 can be reproduced later by reading version 42 - if its
required files/history are still retained. If the team only records 'report ran Tuesday' and uses latest
data on rerun, the result may differ because late-arriving corrections created newer versions.
Persisting relevant version identifiers in job/report metadata dramatically improves reproducibility.
Break it / common failure
Do not promise time travel forever. Do not run VACUUM with aggressively low retention just to save
local disk and then expect old versions to work. Do not confuse reading an old version with restoring
it: a historical read is non-destructive; RESTORE creates a new current commit and can affect
downstream incremental consumers.
Reason through a realistic incident
After an accidental delete, an engineer wants to VACUUM first because storage looks messy. Stop.
Inspect history and verify whether a pre-delete version can still be read. If recovery is required,
choose an explicit restore/rewrite path, reconcile the recovered state and only then revisit retention
cleanup. Maintenance must not destroy your recovery evidence during the incident.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
Version IDs are better operational anchors than wall-clock guesses because clocks, time zones and
delayed commits complicate timestamp reasoning. Still, timestamp travel can be useful when
business processes record times rather than versions. For robust pipelines, capture the input table
version(s), output version and job/run ID together. That forms a lineage breadcrumb even before a
full metadata platform is introduced.
Now you do a changed version alone
Create three versions of a small inventory table. For each version, record version ID, row count,
distinct key count and quantity sum. Write a one-paragraph incident note explaining how you would
reproduce the result of version 1 after version 3 exists.
Fresh changed retry
Assume the table's historical files older than seven days have been vacuumed. Explain what evidence
may remain, what data may no longer be readable, and why a separate backup/compliance strategy
can still be necessary.
Validation and recovery ladder
State the table grain and stable business key before changing data.
Record before/after row count, distinct key count and at least one business total or invariant.
Inspect table history/version evidence; do not infer committed state from physical file presence.
When a source batch can contain multiple rows per target key, make precedence deterministic or
stop on ambiguity.
Repair one cause at a time and rerun a changed case; never hide an unexplained mismatch with
overwrite or dropDuplicates.
Keep protected reviews closed until your genuine attempt and evidence are saved.
Ready-made revision
Time travel reads old snapshots; restore changes current state via a new commit. Historical
availability is bounded by retention and physical files. Record versions as part of reproducible pipeline
evidence.
Evidence / mastery
Save version-specific reconciliations, history output, incident note and retention retry. Be able to
distinguish read-old, restore-old and vacuum-old without mixing them.
Why this matters
Incremental pipelines become dangerous when retrying a batch creates duplicates or when late
changes overwrite newer facts. MERGE lets you express matched/not-matched behavior against a
target table, but MERGE is not automatic idempotency. You still need a stable business key, a
deterministic source batch, duplicate-source protection and a rule for whether an incoming change is
newer/valid. M08 checkpoint discipline and M09 incremental logic now meet a transactional target.
Picture it in your head
Think of a receptionist comparing an incoming change card with a master register. If the key exists,
update only when the card is allowed to supersede the current record. If the key does not exist,
insert. If two cards claim the same key with conflicting values, stop and resolve instead of letting
processing order choose the winner. Re-running the same accepted cards should leave the register
unchanged.
New words before we use them

rows: Conditional table operation combining matched and not-matched actions.
Update an existing key or insert a new key.
Repeating the same logical input produces the same final business state.
Rule that ensures one authoritative source candidate per target key for a merge.
Progress marker used to select incremental source data; it must not outrun durable output.
Change that arrives after newer batches but may carry an older event/update time.

Follow with me once
Run `06_merge_idempotency.py`. The script builds a target orders table and a source batch with one
update and one insert. It first validates one source candidate per order_id. The MERGE updates a
target row only when the source `updated_at` is newer, inserts new keys, then reruns the identical
batch. Save row count, key count and amount sum after first and second runs; they must match.
(target.alias('t').merge(source.alias('s'), 't.order_id = s.order_id')
.whenMatchedUpdate(condition='s.updated_at > t.updated_at', set={
'amount':'s.amount', 'updated_at':'s.updated_at'})
.whenNotMatchedInsertAll().execute())
What you should see
After the first run, the existing order should reflect the newer source value and the new order should
exist once. After rerun, row count, distinct key count and business totals should be unchanged.
History may show an additional MERGE commit even if no business rows change depending on
execution behavior, so idempotency is judged by business state, not by 'no new version ever
appears.'
Why it worked
Target O2 has `updated_at=10:00`, amount 80. Source O2 arrives with `updated_at=10:05`, amount
85, so it may supersede. If a delayed source O2 later arrives with `updated_at=09:55`, a naive
matched-update would roll the table backward. Add a matched condition requiring the source update
to be newer. Then reconcile that the older late batch caused no business regression.
Break it / common failure
Do not feed duplicate source keys into MERGE and assume Delta will choose the latest row for you.
Ambiguous multiple source matches can fail or create nondeterministic logic depending on the
operation/design. Resolve duplicates explicitly before MERGE. Do not advance an upstream
checkpoint before the target commit is durable and validated - M08's candidate-checkpoint pattern
still applies.
Reason through a realistic incident
A nightly job is retried after the orchestrator times out. The first attempt may actually have
committed. The second attempt reprocesses the same source batch. An append-only target doubles
revenue; an idempotent MERGE target should converge to the same key state. Investigate source
batch identity, target history and reconciliation before deciding whether to skip or rerun.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
Idempotency is end-to-end. A perfect MERGE cannot save a pipeline that reads a moving,
nondeterministic source on every retry. Preserve source evidence or a durable batch boundary;
validate source key uniqueness; apply deterministic precedence; commit target; reconcile; only then
commit external progress. This sequence connects ingestion state, transformation state and table
state into one recoverable workflow.
Now you do a changed version alone
Add a second source batch containing one newer update, one stale update and one new key. Predict
target changes, run the merge, then rerun it. Prove key count and totals are stable on retry and the
stale update did not regress the target.
Fresh changed retry
Change the source so two rows share one order_id with different `updated_at` values. Design a
deterministic staging rule that surfaces exact ties as an error rather than arbitrarily ranking them -
reuse the ambiguity discipline from M09.

Record before/after row count, distinct key count and at least one business total or invariant.
Inspect table history/version evidence; do not infer committed state from physical file presence.
When a source batch can contain multiple rows per target key, make precedence deterministic or
stop on ambiguity.
Repair one cause at a time and rerun a changed case; never hide an unexplained mismatch with
overwrite or dropDuplicates.
Keep protected reviews closed until your genuine attempt and evidence are saved.
Ready-made revision
MERGE expresses conditional target changes; idempotency requires deterministic source selection,
stable keys, precedence rules and safe progress commits. Reconcile business state after both first
run and retry.
Evidence / mastery
Save source duplicate check, first-run controls, retry controls, stale-update proof and duplicate-key
retry design. Be ready to explain why 'we use MERGE' is not enough to claim exactly-once business
results.
Why this matters
SCD Type 2 preserves attribute history instead of overwriting it. That matters when analysts need to
know what a customer's region, plan or manager was at the time of a fact. The engineering challenge
is to expire exactly one current row and insert exactly one new current version for a changed
business key, while leaving unchanged keys alone and handling new keys cleanly. Delta MERGE can
support this pattern, but the table grain and temporal invariants must be explicit.
Picture it in your head
Imagine an employee file with transparent sheets. When a person changes department, you do not
erase the old sheet. You mark its valid-to date and place a new sheet on top with a new valid-from
date. At any point there should be one current sheet per employee, and historical sheets must not
overlap in contradictory ways.
New words before we use them

rows: Descriptive entity table such as customer, product, employee.
History-preserving pattern that inserts a new version when tracked attributes change.

lines.text: Effective-from /
effective-to
Validity interval boundaries for each historical version.

rows: Convenience marker identifying the active version.
Warehouse-generated row identifier often used to distinguish historical versions from the stable business key.
Rule such as one current row per business key and non-overlapping validity intervals.

Follow with me once
Run `07_scd2.py`. The fixture starts with current customer versions. The incoming batch contains
one unchanged customer, one changed city and one new customer. The script validates one source
row per customer_id, stages changed rows so the old current version is expired and a new version is
inserted, and inserts the new key. Re-run the same batch to prove no second history row is created
for an unchanged retry.
# Stage changed rows twice: one keyed row expires current target;
# one null merge_key row inserts the new historical version.
# Validate exactly one current row per customer_id after commit.
What you should see
The changed customer should have two versions: one expired historical row and one current row. The
unchanged customer should still have one current row. The new customer should have one current
row. A validation query should prove exactly one current row per business key and no duplicate
effective_from for the same key. Re-running the identical batch should leave these counts
unchanged.
Why it worked
Customer C2 changes city from Patna to Pune effective 2026-09-14. Expire the old C2 row by setting
`effective_to` to the new effective time and `is_current=false`; insert a new C2 row with city Pune,
`effective_from=2026-09-14`, open-ended effective_to and `is_current=true`. Facts dated before the
change can still join to the historical C2 version using the validity interval.
Break it / common failure
Do not update the old row's attributes in place; that destroys history. Do not insert a new current
version without expiring the old one; that produces two current rows. Do not compare every technical
column when detecting change - audit timestamps can create a new version every run. Define the
tracked business attributes deliberately.
Reason through a realistic incident
A dashboard doubles customer counts after an SCD load. Investigation finds two `is_current=true`
rows for some customer_ids because the expire step failed but inserts continued. Treat this as a table
invariant failure, not a dashboard bug. Quarantine/repair the affected load, prove one current row per
key, inspect temporal overlaps, and rerun with transactional/staged logic.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
SCD2 is a model, not a Delta feature. Delta supplies transaction and merge mechanics; you supply
dimensional meaning. In a full warehouse, facts may store surrogate keys resolved at load time, or
joins may use business key plus event timestamp against validity intervals. Both require clean
temporal intervals. Your module goal is not to memorize one clever MERGE statement but to reason
from invariants and validate them after every load.
Now you do a changed version alone
Track `customer_segment` instead of city. Add one changed, one unchanged and one new customer.
Implement/load the change, then write validation queries for one-current-row, no duplicate version
start, and expected historical version counts.
Fresh changed retry
Now receive two changes for the same customer in the same source batch with different effective
times. Explain why the simple one-row-per-key staging contract rejects this batch and what
preprocessing/ordering logic would be required before SCD2 application.
Validation and recovery ladder
State the table grain and stable business key before changing data.
Record before/after row count, distinct key count and at least one business total or invariant.
Inspect table history/version evidence; do not infer committed state from physical file presence.
When a source batch can contain multiple rows per target key, make precedence deterministic or
stop on ambiguity.
Repair one cause at a time and rerun a changed case; never hide an unexplained mismatch with
overwrite or dropDuplicates.
Keep protected reviews closed until your genuine attempt and evidence are saved.
Ready-made revision
SCD2 preserves descriptive history by expiring old versions and inserting new ones. Delta provides
MERGE/transaction mechanics; correctness comes from temporal invariants, deterministic change
detection and source-key discipline.
Evidence / mastery
Save before/after dimension rows, invariant checks, idempotent retry proof and multi-change
reasoning. Explain why one current row per business key is necessary but not sufficient - interval
overlap checks matter too.
Why this matters
Medallion layering is useful when each layer has a clear contract, not when teams create three
folders because a diagram said so. Bronze preserves source evidence with minimal irreversible
transformation. Silver applies validated structure, deduplication, conformance and quality rules. Gold
serves business-ready aggregates or dimensional outputs. The exact names can change, but
separating replayable source evidence from curated business state makes recovery and ownership
clearer.
Picture it in your head
Think of a water-treatment plant. Bronze is the intake reservoir where you preserve what arrived and
when. Silver is the treatment stage where contaminants are identified, rules applied and water
standardized. Gold is the distribution tank prepared for a specific consumer need. You do not pour
Gold back into Bronze or discard intake evidence just because treatment succeeded.
New words before we use them

rows: Raw/landing table layer preserving source fidelity and ingestion metadata.
Validated/conformed layer with explicit quality, typing, dedupe and business-cleaning rules.
Serving layer optimized for business use cases such as aggregates, marts or dimensional outputs.
Ability to rebuild downstream state from preserved upstream evidence.
Explicit place/state for records that fail quality rules without silently disappearing.
Trace of which upstream data and transformations produced an output.

Follow with me once
Run `08_medallion.py`. It writes a Bronze orders table including ingestion metadata and one
deliberately bad row. Silver applies explicit types, key/amount validation and separates invalid
records into a quarantine table instead of dropping them silently. Gold aggregates valid Silver rows
by business date. Reconcile counts across Bronze = Silver-valid + quarantine, then reconcile Gold
amount totals back to Silver.
assert bronze_count == silver_count + quarantine_count
assert round(silver_sales, 2) == round(gold_sales, 2)
What you should see
Every Bronze row must be accounted for either in valid Silver output or quarantine. Gold totals must
equal the corresponding Silver valid totals for the metric definition. The layers should be separate
Delta tables/paths, with Bronze evidence retained. A Gold aggregate should not become the only
copy of detailed business facts.
Why it worked
If Bronze has 6 rows, one with negative quantity, Silver may contain 5 valid rows and quarantine 1
rejected row. Gold daily revenue should aggregate the 5 valid rows only. Your control equation is 6 =
5 + 1, plus `sum(Silver.gross_sales) = sum(Gold.daily_sales)`. That simple reconciliation is more
trustworthy than saying 'the notebook ran green.'
Break it / common failure
Do not transform Bronze so heavily that original source evidence is lost. Do not let Silver silently drop
rows without a reconciliation path. Do not build Gold directly from raw sources when Silver defines
the canonical cleaning/conformance rules unless the exception is deliberate and documented. And do
not assume Bronze/Silver/Gold means three copies of every dataset forever; retention and design
depend on requirements.
Reason through a realistic incident
A Gold KPI is 4% lower than source finance totals. Start at Gold-to-Silver reconciliation, then
Silver-to-Bronze/quarantine, then Bronze-to-source manifest. You may discover an intentional quality
rejection, a duplicate rule, a late source batch or a Gold filter. Layering helps because each boundary
has a contract and control total; without that, engineers jump randomly across notebooks.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
Medallion design is strongest when paired with idempotent rebuild rules. If Silver can be
deterministically rebuilt from immutable/preserved Bronze evidence, incident recovery becomes
simpler. Gold can then be rebuilt from stable Silver. This is not always free - large histories cost
storage/compute - so production designs balance replay window, retention and recovery objectives.
Keep the course pattern simple and explicit before adding streaming/change-data-feed complexity in
Now you do a changed version alone
Design Bronze/Silver/Gold for parcel scans. State one-row grain, keys, retained raw fields, Silver
quality rules, quarantine behavior, Gold consumer and two reconciliation equations. Then implement
one small variant using the practice scaffold.
Fresh changed retry
Now add a GDPR deletion requirement. Explain which layers and historical copies may be affected
and why a simple 'delete from Gold' is not a complete governance response.
Validation and recovery ladder
State the table grain and stable business key before changing data.
Record before/after row count, distinct key count and at least one business total or invariant.
Inspect table history/version evidence; do not infer committed state from physical file presence.
When a source batch can contain multiple rows per target key, make precedence deterministic or
stop on ambiguity.
Repair one cause at a time and rerun a changed case; never hide an unexplained mismatch with
overwrite or dropDuplicates.
Keep protected reviews closed until your genuine attempt and evidence are saved.
Ready-made revision
Bronze preserves source evidence, Silver creates validated/conformed truth, Gold serves business
use. The value is clear contracts and replay/reconciliation, not the medal names themselves.
Evidence / mastery
Save layer schemas, Bronze/Silver/quarantine counts, Silver/Gold totals, design note and privacy
retry. Be able to trace one Gold number back to source evidence.
Why this matters
Reliable tables can still become slow or expensive if every tiny batch creates many small files.
Compaction combines smaller files into better-sized files without changing business rows. VACUUM is
different: it physically removes unreferenced files beyond retention, reducing storage but potentially
eliminating old-version readability. Maintenance must preserve business results and respect
recovery/concurrency requirements. Performance work never gets permission to erase evidence
casually.
Picture it in your head
Picture a library. Compaction is rebinding many thin pamphlets into fewer well-organized volumes
while keeping the same text. VACUUM is throwing away withdrawn old editions after the retention
policy says they are no longer needed. One changes layout; the other changes what historical
physical material remains available.
New words before we use them

rows: Too many small data files create metadata/opening overhead and inefficient scans.
Rewrite layout into fewer/larger files while preserving table rows.
Delta command/API for file compaction; can return metrics.
Remove unreferenced data files older than retention threshold.
Minimum age for eligible unreferenced files; must exceed safety/recovery needs.
Metadata concept indicating whether a commit represents business data changes versus layout-only actions.

Follow with me once
Run `09_maintenance.py` only in the disposable learner table. The script creates several small
append commits, records row/key/amount controls and table detail, runs Delta
`optimize().executeCompaction()`, then reruns the same business controls. It prints the safe VACUUM
command as a learning reference but does not execute destructive shortened-retention cleanup. Use
default/safe retention in real practice unless you fully understand the consequences.
delta = DeltaTable.forPath(spark, str(TABLE))
metrics = delta.optimize().executeCompaction()
metrics.show(truncate=False)
# VACUUM is intentionally not run with unsafe short retention in this course.
What you should see
Business row count, distinct keys and totals must be identical before and after compaction. File
metrics may improve. A second compaction may do little because bin-packing is designed to be
idempotent for unchanged data. No course script should disable retention safety merely to
demonstrate deletion.
Why it worked
A table has 2,000 tiny files from micro-batches. Compaction may replace them with fewer larger files
in a new table version while keeping the same rows. Old files can remain physically present until
VACUUM eligibility. If you immediately measure raw directory size, it may temporarily increase even
though current query layout improved. Distinguish current active files from retained historical files.
Break it / common failure
Do not equate OPTIMIZE with removing duplicates; it changes physical layout, not business grain. Do
not use VACUUM as a performance fix for bad query plans. Do not disable retention checks or set
zero-hour retention in a beginner lab. Do not run maintenance during an unresolved corruption
incident when historical versions may be needed for comparison/recovery.
Reason through a realistic incident
Storage cost spikes after a series of overwrites. An engineer proposes aggressive VACUUM. First
inspect history, active file metrics, retention policy, longest-running readers/streams and recovery
requirements. Maybe old files are legitimately retained; maybe compaction is needed; maybe the
pipeline rewrites too much. Choose maintenance only after identifying the cause.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
Maintenance has three separate objectives: read performance/layout, storage cleanup and historical
recoverability. They can conflict. A platform may optimize layout frequently but vacuum
conservatively. Record maintenance operations in operational evidence and monitor their metrics. In
cloud object storage, file count can affect listing/metadata overhead even when total bytes are
modest; in local training, we simulate the reasoning at small scale without pretending it benchmarks
production.
Now you do a changed version alone
Create 10 tiny append commits in a disposable table. Record history count, detail/file metrics and
business controls. Compact, then reconcile business state. Write a proposed VACUUM retention policy
for a hypothetical daily pipeline with a 3-day maximum outage/recovery window and explain your
safety margin.
Fresh changed retry
Change the system so a streaming consumer can lag for five days. Explain how that changes
retention thinking and why a generic '7 days is always enough' rule is not engineering reasoning.

State the table grain and stable business key before changing data.
Record before/after row count, distinct key count and at least one business total or invariant.
Inspect table history/version evidence; do not infer committed state from physical file presence.
When a source batch can contain multiple rows per target key, make precedence deterministic or
stop on ambiguity.
Repair one cause at a time and rerun a changed case; never hide an unexplained mismatch with
overwrite or dropDuplicates.
Keep protected reviews closed until your genuine attempt and evidence are saved.
Ready-made revision
OPTIMIZE changes layout; VACUUM removes eligible unreferenced physical files. Both require
before/after evidence, but only VACUUM can destroy old-version readability. Never trade
recoverability for a demo shortcut.
Evidence / mastery
Save pre/post compaction controls, metrics/history, retention proposal and lag retry. State clearly
whether live OPTIMIZE/VACUUM was executed or only reviewed on your machine.
Why this matters
The module is complete only when you can connect the pieces under failure: preserve a replayable
source boundary, write Bronze, validate and curate Silver, apply idempotent MERGE/SCD behavior
where needed, serve Gold, inspect history, reproduce an older version, and separate layout
maintenance from business correction. The integrated checkpoint is deliberately small enough for a
laptop but uses the same reasoning order you will need in production.
Picture it in your head
Picture an evidence chain rather than a pile of scripts: source batch -> Bronze commit -> Silver
validation/quarantine -> curated Delta commit -> Gold output -> reconciliations -> history/version
IDs -> run record. If something breaks, move along the chain and find the first boundary where
expected and actual state diverge. Do not start by randomly changing Spark settings.

Independent comparison proving populations/totals are preserved or intentionally changed.
Known source/table version from which the pipeline can safely replay/rebuild.

The evidence summary should contain source/Bronze/Silver/Gold counts, key counts, business totals,

preserve curated row/key/totals. If live Delta is unavailable, the pure-Python

Why it worked
Suppose the second run produces one extra curated row. Work backward: Did source batch identity
change? Did the staging query duplicate a key? Did MERGE use the stable business key? Did a Bronze
append occur twice but Silver dedupe fail? Which reconciliation first diverged? The fastest debugger
follows controls, not intuition. Table history tells you what committed; source/run metadata tells you
why the job attempted it.
Break it / common failure
Do not call the checkpoint complete because every script exited zero. Deliberately break one case:
duplicate source key, invalid amount, stale update or schema drift. Save the first failure, diagnose it,
repair one cause, rerun and prove reconciliation. Do not hide the error by dropDuplicates without a
deterministic rule or by overwriting the whole table.
Reason through a realistic incident
At 08:00 Gold revenue is wrong. Bronze count matches source manifest. Silver valid + quarantine
matches Bronze, but Silver revenue is too high. That narrows the failure to Silver
transformation/dedupe rather than ingestion. Inspect key uniqueness and merge staging before
touching Gold. If the wrong Silver commit is isolated and history retained, use time travel to compare
versions and build a corrected forward commit/recovery plan.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
A production lakehouse is an operational system, not a storage slogan. The strongest habit from M13
is to treat every table change as a state transition with evidence: intended input, deterministic
transformation, transactional commit, independent reconciliation, history/version capture and safe
progress. M14 will add streaming/event-driven behavior, where the same state discipline becomes
even more important because retries and continuous processing amplify weak assumptions.

Run the integrated checkpoint with a changed batch that includes a new key, a newer correction, one
invalid row and one unchanged retry. Produce a one-page run report: source batch ID, counts, key

amounts. The correct outcome is to surface ambiguity and stop before target progress. Explain why
choosing whichever row appears last would make retries/order changes unsafe.

stop on ambiguity.
Repair one cause at a time and rerun a changed case; never hide an unexplained mismatch with
overwrite or dropDuplicates.
Keep protected reviews closed until your genuine attempt and evidence are saved.
Ready-made revision
A trustworthy lakehouse pipeline is a chain of deterministic state transitions with preserved source
evidence, transactional table commits, reconciliation and recoverable history. Debug the first
boundary where controls diverge.
Evidence / mastery
Save the integrated run report, live commands/results, one deliberate failure, recovery proof,
idempotent retry and 90-second teach-back. If any runtime step was not executed on your learner PC,
label it PENDING instead of converting static/simulator QA into mastery.
